newsitem.title: FRANCE: Thomson-CSF selloff could hit legal snag.
newsitem.headline: Thomson-CSF selloff could hit legal snag.

text.p: France's privatisation of defence electronics group Thomson-CSF could hit a legal hitch on Friday, which would delay the procedure but would not make the sale impossible, La Tribune newspaper said on Wednesday.

On Friday, the Council of State, France's highest administrative court, will rule on whether the government can sell its 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF using a 1991 law or whether it has to follow the privatisation law of 1986.
According to La Tribune, the court will say the government has to follow the earlier law and will have to publish a decree indicating whether the sale will be a public sale or a private placement.
Court officials were not immediately available for comment.

The main difference between the two laws, apart from the legal ramifications, is that the procedure using the 1986 law is slower than the one using the 1991 act and the government had wanted to move quickly on the Thomson-CSF sale to offset the bad impression made when it suspended the sale of Thomson SA early in December.

The government decided in October that it wanted to sell Thomson SA, which has a 58-percent stake in Thomson-CSF and 100 percent of consumer electronics group Thomson Multimedia (TMM) to Lagardere Groupe.
The state had to abandon the plans after France's independent Privatisation Commission said it objected to terms of the sale by Lagardere of TMM to Daewoo Electronics of South Korea.
Lagardere planned to bid for the 42 percent of Thomson-CSF listed on the Paris Bourse and merge the company with its own Matra Defense Espace unit.

Noel Forgeard, chairman of the Matra unit which has a missile joint venture with British Aerospace Plc, told Les Echos newspaper on Wednesday that he was against a public sale of the Thomson-CSF stake.

Thomson has declined comment on newspaper reports that its management, led by chairman Marcel Roulet, prefers a public sale on the share market over a private placement with another company -- Lagardere, Alcatel Alsthom or any another.
"What some are recommending, floating the stake owned by the state in Thomson-CSF, would not expand but freeze the industrial boundaries of Thomson," Forgeard said.
He warned that with a float there could be a core group of different shareholders whose differing agendas could lead to the break-up of Thomson-CSF.
Government sources said that it would announce in early January how it wants to proceed with the privatisation of the Thomson group.
